h1: Ageing Belgian quadrupel and strong dark ales at home
title: Ageing Belgian Quadrupel at Home | Craft Beer School
desc: How Belgian quadrupels and strong dark ales change with age, how long to keep them and how to store them in an Indian home.
teaser: A quad at ten months and at three years are different beers. Here is what happens in between.
standfirst: Belgian quadrupels and other strong dark ales are some of the best beers to age at home. We explain what changes in the bottle, how long to wait and when the beer starts to fade.
sections:
A Belgian quadrupel is a strong, dark ale, usually around 10% ABV, with a rich malt base, dark candi sugar and a fruity, spicy Belgian yeast character. Most are bottle conditioned, so a little live yeast sits in the bottle. High alcohol, residual sweetness and dark malt all slow the effects of oxygen and give the beer something to change into.

The same logic covers other strong dark ales: Belgian dark strong ales, barley wines and old ales. A 5% pale ale has nothing in reserve. A 10% quad does.

Fresh, a quad can taste sweet and hot, with banana and clove esters and a sharp alcohol edge. Over the first year or two several things happen at once:

  • The alcohol heat softens and reads as warmth.
  • Fresh fruity esters fade.
  • Slow oxidation builds dried fruit notes: raisin, fig, prune and later sherry.
  • Sweetness appears to drop and the beer tastes rounder.

With more years you may find leather and tobacco notes, especially in beers stored cool. Carbonation can also drift up or down depending on the yeast and the seal.

Three slow processes drive the change. The first is oxidation. Even a well-sealed bottle has a little oxygen in the headspace and more creeps in through the seal over time. It reacts with malt and hop compounds to give the dried fruit, sherry and eventually papery notes.

The second is the Maillard reaction, which keeps going very slowly at cellar temperature. It deepens colour a touch and adds toasty, caramel-like notes. The third is the yeast. Live yeast in a bottle-conditioned quad can take up a little oxygen and may slowly change the beer's carbonation and ester profile. Over many years it can also start to break down, which in warm storage gives meaty or soy-like notes.

Temperature controls the speed of all three. That is why the same beer can taste beautifully mature in one home and tired in another after the same number of months.

There is no fixed answer, which is why we suggest buying several bottles. As a rough guide, most quads show a clear change between one and three years. Some well-known examples are still drinking well at five years or more when stored cool. Beyond that, results vary a lot from bottle to bottle.

Watch the first signs of decline: a thin, papery note, a flat finish or a body that tastes watery rather than round. When your notes show those, open the rest soon. Our guide on telling when an aged beer has gone past its best covers the warning signs.
Storing them in an Indian home

Strong dark ales are forgiving but not heatproof. Aim for 10 to 15 °C, dark and steady. Keep crown-capped bottles upright so the yeast settles in a small ring at the bottom and the beer has less contact with the cap. Light is a real risk in clear or green glass, so keep bottles in their boxes or a closed cupboard.

If you have no cool space, a quad stored at 28 to 30 °C will race through its changes. It will taste aged in months and tired within a year or so. A small wine fridge set to about 13 °C is the best spend for a serious home cellar. Our guide to cellar temperature and humidity has the detail.

Stand the bottle upright for a day before opening. Chill to about 12 to 14 °C, not fridge cold, because cold mutes the dried fruit and malt depth you waited for. Use a chalice or tulip. Pour slowly in one motion and stop before the yeast layer.

Share it. A 330 ml bottle at 10% ABV carries a lot of alcohol, so pour small measures for three or four people, drink water alongside and plan your ride home.

The most useful thing you can do is taste a young and an old bottle of the same beer side by side. The differences jump out in a way no description can match. Write down the colour, aroma, sweetness, alcohol and finish for each.

The gap most people find is naming what they taste. "It is smoother" is true but tells you little. Being able to say that esters dropped while sherry rose is what lets you predict how the next bottle will go.

Your first step: buy three bottles of one quad this month. Open one now, write five lines and put the other two away in the coolest dark corner you have.
faqs: How long can you age a Belgian quadrupel?
Most show clear changes between one and three years and some are still good at five years or more when stored cool and dark. Results vary by beer and by storage.
What temperature should I store quads at?
Around 10 to 15 °C, dark and steady. Warmer storage speeds ageing so much that the beer can tire within a year.
Should I age quads upright or on their side?
Crown-capped bottles are best stored upright so the yeast settles at the bottom and the beer touches the cap less.
